Name: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
Description:
Founded in 1936, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory is a federally funded research and development center managed for NASA by the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
 
For nearly nine decades, JPL has helped define the frontier of exploration. The laboratory developed America's first Earth-orbiting science satellite, built the first successful interplanetary spacecraft, and pioneered robotic exploration across the solar system. These achievements helped establish U.S. leadership in space and laid the foundation for generations of scientific discovery.
 
Today, on behalf of NASA and the nation, JPL advances science and innovation through robotic missions that explore Earth, the solar system, and the universe. Our engineers, scientists, technologists, and mission teams continue to push the boundaries of exploration while addressing scientific and technical challenges of national significance.
 
We Dare Mighty Things.

Visit http://jpl.jobs to explore our career opportunities.

Name: Spacebourne
Description:
Spacebourne Inc. is an aerospace AI company building the intelligence and compute infrastructure for the next era of space operations. Our two-platform strategy addresses the most pressing constraints in the orbital environment today and tomorrow.

CLARITY (Cognitive Link Analytics for RF Interference TrajectorY) is our operational ML-powered SaaS platform that predicts satellite RF interference up to 72 hours in advance, delivering actionable recommendations for frequency hops, power adjustments, and maneuver windows before disruptions occur. Currently in active beta with one of the world's top three ground station networks, CLARITY shifts operators from reactive monitoring to predictive control.

GALILEO Cube is our CubeSat platform in development, engineered to deploy GPU-accelerated AI inference directly in orbit using an NVIDIA Jetson compute module, solar power harvesting, and passive radiative cooling. Targeted for first launch in 2027, GALILEO advances the long-term GALILEO Centers vision: modular orbital compute infrastructure that processes data where it is generated, eliminating the bandwidth and latency constraints of ground-based processing as the space economy scales.

CLARITY proves the intelligence. GALILEO extends it into orbit. Together, they represent a single, coherent thesis: the operators who will win in the new space economy need infrastructure that is as intelligent as the missions it supports. Spacebourne is building that infrastructure.

Name: SpaceValley Foundation
Description:
Space Valley Region
Located along the Rio Grande River corridor from southern New Mexico to southern Colorado, Space Valley stands as a pioneering center for scientific inquiry, space exploration, and deep technology innovation. With a storied past as the birthplace of modern rocketry and a history steeped in groundbreaking discoveries, Space Valley merges scientific excellence with human experience to ignite visionary breakthroughs and inspire transformative solutions.

Here, bold vision, cutting-edge science, rich cultural heritage, and diverse voices converge in a dynamic environment that fosters creativity, discovery, and ingenuity. The region’s powerful landscapes and collaborative spirit spark the big ideas needed to tackle the world’s most complex challenges—and shape the future of space.

As a catalyst for global progress, Space Valley brings together the military, business, and public sectors in an incubative environment that supports the earliest stages of innovation. This fusion of advanced technology, technical expertise, cultural wisdom, and entrepreneurial energy powers a thriving community where history and innovation intertwine to change the world.

SpaceValley Foundation
Founded in 2024, SpaceValley Foundation, based in Albuquerque, New Mexico, connects diverse people, ideas, and interests in a singular mission to unlock the transformative power of space to benefit the Space Valley community and humanity as a whole.

As the space industry becomes increasingly relevant to a wider range of people and industries, the foundation optimizes the Space Valley region’s ability to harness this growth by systematically:

Connecting community to build transparency and partnership
Promoting Space Valley stakeholders and their work
Uniting non-space organizations with space opportunities
Cultivating awareness of space and its value to humanity.

Description:

We operate at the intersection of space technology, art, and design—bringing space down to Earth through tangible, real-world experiences and solutions.

Our work spans concept to production. We launched and successfully funded a Kickstarter campaign for the first patented women’s space travel suit, featuring a novel dropseat design that enables bathroom access without disrobing. The suit has been field tested in analog environments, including wear testing by astronauts at the Mars Desert Research Station, CAMões Lab, and Habitat Marte. We led the full development lifecycle—from design and prototyping to materials selection, fit validation, and small-batch production. This work has been featured in National Geographic, Essence, WWD, Nice Kicks, and other major publications.

We also develop speculative and applied wearable systems for science and public engagement, including the Astra Matra Suit, presented at the Hay Festival and the Royal Institution.

GISC leads STEMulating Art, a youth-focused program that brings space, science, and engineering into creative practice. Through hands-on kits and workshops, students learn physics by building, designing, and storytelling—meeting them where they are and expanding who sees themselves as part of the future of space.

We extend this work through mentorship and workforce development, guiding high school interns on real-world engineering and design projects with a focus on problem definition, prototyping, and systems-level thinking.

We have a proven record of solving complex problems for our customers. Our analysis and design recommendations have resulted in reduced cost and downtime, as well as a better understanding of the physics to improve future designs. Our headquarters is located just outside of Philadelphia in Pipersville, PA. We also have a remote office in Huntsville, AL.

CRAFT Tech specializes in the high-fidelity computational simulation of complex fluid dynamic and combustion problems on large-scale, parallel architecture computers. Services we provide to government and industry include the analysis of complex design problems including: combustion and multi-component mixtures, unsteady relative motion, multi-phase (cavitating) flows, acoustics, and turbomachinery. In addition, we provide technical consultation and on-site services. We also license software that specialize in modeling complex physics and thermochemistry. Finally, we perform fundamental research in CFD, grid adaptation, aeroacoustics, turbulence, combustion and multi-phase flow.

Its mission is to advance experimental approaches to propulsion, focusing on engineering and practical demonstrations as much as on theoretical models.

What makes APEC distinctive is its diverse mix of participants. The event regularly features PhD researchers and professionals from organizations such as NASA, DARPA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, and MIT, alongside garage experimenters, hobbyists, and entrepreneurs. This cross-pollination of ideas between institutional experts and independent builders creates a fertile ground for innovation, blending scientific rigor with imaginative experimentation.

The topics presented at APEC are as bold as its community. Discussions often center on gravity modification, warp drives, inertial propulsion, electrogravitics, field-effect propulsion systems, and zero-point energy. In recent years, APEC has also incorporated sessions on the physics of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP), reflecting broader scientific and public interest in anomalous flight technologies. Presentations range from highly technical papers to live demonstrations of experimental hardware, offering a rare mix of visionary science and hands-on engineering.

APEC has been described by the media as the “Woodstock of gravity-modification research” and the “wildest science club on the internet.” Its 2023 return after a brief hiatus reinvigorated the community, with talks covering electromagnetic propulsion, propellantless drives, and speculative warp reactor concepts.

Research Thrusts:
What is the global structure of the heliosphere? 
How do pickup ions evolve from cradle to grave, and how do they affect heliospheric processes?
How does the heliosphere interact with and influence the interstellar medium? 
How are cosmic rays filtered by and transported through the heliosphere?

Benefits and potential impacts of successful research:
The heliosphere is an immense shield that protects the solar system from harsh galactic radiation. This radiation affects both life on Earth and human space exploration. The heliosphere is a window into processes occurring in all other astrospheres. Understanding these processes enables predictions about the astrospheric conditions necessary to create habitable planets.

Description:
In the realm of space exploration and future Mars settlement, the importance of a plant-based diet cannot be overstated. As humanity ventures further into the cosmos, optimizing resources and ensuring the survival of both astronauts and the land they inhabit become paramount considerations. Embracing a plant-based diet offers a myriad of benefits that align closely with the objectives of space exploration and Mars settlement.

First and foremost, a plant-based diet is inherently more resource-efficient compared to traditional animal-based diets. Plant-based foods require significantly less water, land, and energy to produce, making them ideal candidates for space missions where resources are limited and must be carefully managed. By shifting towards plant-based diets, space agencies can reduce the logistical burden of transporting food supplies from Earth, thereby enabling longer-duration missions and more sustainable space exploration endeavors.

Moreover, plant-based diets align seamlessly with the development of future biological life support systems, which are essential for long-duration space missions and Mars settlement. These closed-loop environmental systems aim to create self-sustaining ecosystems where waste products are recycled and reused to support plant growth and human habitation. By incorporating plant-based diets into these systems, astronauts can utilize the byproducts of plant cultivation to nourish both themselves and the ecosystem, fostering a harmonious relationship between humans and their environment in space.

Research conducted with all-vegan analog astronaut crews plays a crucial role in advancing our understanding of the dietary requirements and nutritional needs of astronauts in space. By studying the physiological and psychological effects of plant-based diets in simulated space environments, scientists can develop tailored dietary protocols that optimize health, performance, and well-being during space missions.

Name: Great Lunar Expedition for Everyone (GLEE)
Description:

The Great Lunar Expedition for Everyone (GLEE) is a pioneering space mission opening the lunar frontier to the next generation of scientists. Led by Principal Investigator Barbra Sobhani at CU Boulder, GLEE is supported by the Colorado Space Grant Consortium (COSGC), NASA, and the Artemis program.

The Mission & Technology
GLEE flies as a hosted payload on a commercial lunar lander. Using an autonomous Housing Deployment Module (HDM), we deploy a distributed network of palm-sized "ChipSats" (LunaSats) across the Moon's surface. Operating for six lunar hours (seven Earth days), these compact sensor pucks form a wireless mesh network for time-resolved data collection.

Each LunaSat is an independent node addressing NASA Decadal survey needs. Using a swarm approach, GLEE maps thermal gradients, regolith capacitance, crustal magnetic fields, and impact data across a wide area without single-point telemetry bias.

Global Impact & STEM Education
GLEE is about inclusion. Using cost-effective materials, we build outreach kits with a $250 target cost, empowering students with no prior coding experience to participate.

Global Scale: GLEE supports 242+ student teams and 2,000+ students across 29 US states and 30+ countries.

LEAP Modules: Our curriculum guides teams through a mission's full lifecycle—from idea formation to proposal writing—covering sensors, power, and RF communication.

Hands-on Learning: Teams configure their hardware, define localized science cases, and access open-source lunar telemetry via our public dashboard.

Validated: less than 2% mean absolute error estimating 7 independent parameters from 2 sensor outputs alone.

Applications span aerospace, defense, robotics, semiconductor manufacturing, energy production, multiphase flow systems, and autonomous vehicles.

Our focus areas include propellantless propulsion devices utilizing a variety of reactionless drive principles. Some of these are based on known physics, and for others our research team is pushing the boundaries of physics to develop new principles.

Name: RAIN Lab
Description:
Our group’s research focuses on analyzing and synthesizing networked distributed autonomous systems operating in complex environments. We examine fundamental and theoretical questions at the intersection of control theory, optimization, networks, guidance, navigation, and control issues for space, air, and ground robotic systems.

As networks become ubiquitous in many areas of engineering, it has become of paramount importance to examine how the network and its structure affect the dynamic properties of the overall system, such as its stability, performance, and robustness, both in the random and deterministic settings. We also consider some of the more fundamental system-theoretic questions such as controllability and observability of networked systems. Our research team examines a wide range of questions from a theoretical point of view as well as their ramifications for systems such as multiple spacecraft formation flying, networked robotics, UAV formations, heterogenous dynamic networks, and more recently, in the setting of social and molecular networks.

Another facet of our research deals with the operation of autonomous vehicular systems in complex environments, such as guidance laws for spacecraft attitude control in nonconvex constraints, trajectory planning for solar-powered unmanned aerial vehicles, and formation flight. Large-scale optimization for the operation of dynamic systems provides yet another facet of our research, with particular applications to energy management and green technologies.

The underlying design principle is the aggressive removal of work from the user to handle deterministic implementaion details required to access, use, parse, or visualize data. It is in this way our interfaces allow the user to focus on understanding what the data are saying – the science, reducing the time to discovery.

Muna also has extensive teaching experience having created SciCoder (http://scicoder.org), an intensive five day data science workshop aimed at early career researchers. Over 14 workshops have been run at institutions such as NYU, Yale, the American Museum of Natural History, and as far away as Perth, Australia.

The company is built on top of 20+ years of professional research, software development, project management, interface design, and teaching experience. Description:
Lillie Earth Intelligence builds satellite intelligence for the infrastructure a nation depends on.

Crude theft, illegal refining, spills and encroachment cost Nigeria more than 2 billion dollars a year. The people who have to act on it rely on slow, costly and dangerous patrols. Ordinary camera satellites are defeated by the Niger Delta's cloud cover and by darkness. Nobody watches the whole corridor.

We set a baseline for an area, then screen it with multiple independent satellite sensors: radar, thermal, optical, vegetation, gas and water temperature. Radar is the all-weather backbone, so cloud and darkness do not stop the watch. We raise a candidate only where separate sensors agree. The output is decision ready: a ranked worklist of where to look first, situation reports, and sealed evidence packs.

Our watch is persistent and revisit-based. It is not a live feed. New observations arrive when a satellite next passes overhead. Every detection is an advisory candidate for analyst verification, never a confirmed event. We state this plainly because the people who act on our work deserve to know exactly what they are holding.

LillieWatch is our onshore product for energy infrastructure. LillieOre applies the same engine to solid minerals and illegal mining, reconciled against the national mining cadastre. LillieTriton addresses offshore platforms and the Exclusive Economic Zone.

About Us
The Colorado Space Grant Consortium is a state-wide program that provides Colorado students access to space through innovative courses, real-world hands-on satellite programs, and interactive outreach programs. There are 52 consortia in the National Space Grant program, with one consortium in each state, in addition to Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C.

Our vision:
Providing an inclusive and interdisciplinary community of Colorado students with experiences in space to prepare them for our Nation’s future space programs.

Our mission:
COSGC uses the excitement of our Nation’s aeronautics and space program to inspire, educate, and develop America’s future technological workforce by enabling an inclusive and interdisciplinary community of college and university students to participate in space-based hands-on projects, courses, research, and public service activities.

The COSGC involves 21 colleges, universities and institutions around Colorado. Each year COSGC engages over 300 college and university students. Many of our members teach space-related courses.

The COSGC headquarters is located in the Discovery Learning Center on the campus of the University of Colorado at Boulder. Each affiliate institution has a Director who oversees student programs on their home campuses, in addition to faculty, industry, and community mentors..

Name: Astrum Drive Aerospace
Description:
Astrum Drive Technologies is a forward-thinking US-based space startup focused on developing advanced propulsion systems. Our team has developed a groundbreaking propulsion system that directly converts electrical energy into continuous thrust, eliminating the need for conventional fuels. 
This breakthrough enables deep space travel, significantly extends satellite lifespans, boosts spacecraft range, speed, and payload capacity, and lowers operational costs - benefiting satellite operators, space agencies, and defense organizations alike. 
With proven prototypes, secured patents, and partnerships with leading universities & space companies, we are poised to redefine the future of space travel.

Our propellantless propulsion technology offers significant advantages for satellite applications. By eliminating the need for onboard fuel storage, satellites equipped with our system can be lighter, more compact, and have extended operational lifetimes. This technology enables the satellites to perform efficient orbital maneuvers, precise station-keeping, and opens up new possibilities for satellite constellations and formations.

Our research is published in prestigious Q1 journals, we have LOIs and collaborations with leading US institutions, including the University of Alabama in Huntsville, NASA, SpaceX and others.

Detection of minerals such as gold, lithium, copper, iron, and rare earth elements

 Value

Name: Artera
Description:
The pantry doesn't launch with you anymore.

Every mission today is scoped around a shrinking pantry instead of the exploration itself. As long as food has to be launched, stored and resupplied on a fixed schedule, the range of every mission collapses to the size of what it can carry.

Artera grows food in space with a constellation of autonomous agriculture pods — positioned and orbited to meet missions where they're going.

Not one farm. A living constellation. Pods hold a ring of low orbits in each neighborhood, clustered around Earth and the Moon, with Mars as the network extends outward. Each pod tends its own harvest and flies its own trajectory — deciding where and how to grow across the network, and how to navigate each harvest to you. Crops are cultivated from compact supplies aboard the pods, turning launched mass into a renewing harvest instead of a shrinking pantry. The agronomy and the flight dynamics are ours to solve — never yours.

For you, it's just grocery delivery. Choose what to order, and Artera calculates the rest from your mission, outpost, space station or off-world settlement — growing it and routing it automatically, then delivering fresh food on a schedule you can count on. A menu, not a mission plan. That is the whole interface. The complexity is real. It's just not yours.

We're an early-stage team out of Space City, building the food supply chain in space. The constellation is proposed, the work is underway, and we publish what we measure — including what doesn't work yet.

Addresses critical gaps in today’s wireless ecosystem. While 5G and millimeter-wave technologies promise high throughput, they face inherent limitations in coverage, penetration, spectrum availability, reliability, and infrastructure cost. Dense small-cell deployments, limited sub-6 GHz spectrum, poor performance through buildings, and vulnerability to environmental conditions constrain truly ubiquitous connectivity. Satellite systems offer alternatives but remain susceptible to solar activity and ionospheric disturbances that can disrupt navigation, timing, financial systems, and critical infrastructure.

Pioneering a spectrum-independent, post-RF communication technology based on Longitudinal Circular Polarization Magnetic Waves (LCPMW). Unlike conventional RF systems, this approach operates without electric-field radiation, generating magneto-acoustic waves that are resilient to interference, deeply penetrating through materials, and unaffected by solar energetic particles.

Economic impact: reduced infrastructure density, lower deployment costs, and improved resilience for IoT, autonomous vehicles, V2X, and critical systems.
Social impact: enhanced connectivity in underserved, underground, industrial, and disaster-prone environments, improving safety, mobility, and digital inclusion.
Technology benefits: spectrum coexistence, immunity to RF congestion and solar disruptions, and a complementary path toward 6G and beyond.

Building resilient, sustainable, and inclusive connectivity where communication works everywhere, even when RF cannot.

UASPACE's BAMA-1 CubeSat was selected for the NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative in 2020 and was aboard the Astra LV-0008 vehicle for the failed attempt on February 10, 2022. BAMA-2 will be a re-build and re-flight effort of BAMA-1. Due to the unfortunate mission failure during launch, NASA has given us a second opportunity to build and launch our BAMA-2 CubeSAT through the NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative. We aim to have a fully built and functional satellite by May 2023.

BAMA-2 is a technology demonstration mission that will conduct a flight demonstration of a drag sail module by rapidly deorbiting the satellite. Spacecraft equipped with drag sail technology will be able to reliably and rapidly deorbit, thus reducing space debris and the risk to operational satellites, space stations, and crewed vehicles.

Name: O ANALYTICS INCORPORATED
Description:
COMPANY FOCUS: O Analytics is a premier space object characterization company applying signal processing, physics-based techniques, and machine learning (ML) to detect, classify and characterize satellites and orbital debris. Our experienced team of computer science, physics, machine learning, astrophysics and data science experts with 40+ combined years in digital signal processing and information science is committed to ensuring safety and protection of assets orbiting the Earth.

O ANALYTICS SOLUTION: Our innovative Deep Learning Track Analytics (DELTA) quickly answers important questions about active and inoperable satellites – such as What is it? What is it doing? and What is it likely to do next? Our core solution combines convolution, machine learning and physics-based technology to detect and characterize space objects – fast and agnostically. Our solution involves tuning to the sensor environment versus time consuming and arduous AI training, processes with low resource consumption, and is adaptable to new and emerging sensing technologies. O Analytics is also developing a comprehensive space object custody management system (SOCMS) that addresses the critical question - What are objects likely to do next?

CUSTOMERS/USE: Military, civil, and intelligence agencies; and commercial space asset owners. Especially useful for ISR, space domain awareness, satellite fleet custody management, space traffic management, rendezvous proximity operations and collision avoidance.

TECHNOLOGY STATUS: Our patent-pending DELTA algorithmic software combines Newtonian physics principles, correlation inference, and real-time multi-hypothesis Markov tracking techniques to detect, conclusively classify and characterize pattern of life behavior of space objects. DELTA is designed to trigger downstream Deep Neural Network (DNN) AI/ML, sensor tasking and other processes that support autonomous or person-in-the-loop operations with an underlying goal of providing awareness.

Name: Ram Accelerator Research Group
Description:
To enable human exploration and survivability in space, we must develop the means to deliver payloads to orbit at a greater capacity than rockets are capable of. The technology that can do this is the Ram Accelerator.

Consider that the mass of a rocket payload is less than 8%, whereas with a ram accelerator the mass of the payload could be 19-50% according to some estimates.
The purpose of the Ram Accelerator Research Program is to solve the remaining engineering problems needed to bring the ram accelerator to the forefront of payload delivery to orbit.

At present the United States has ram accelerator research facilities at the University of Washington in Seattle and Southeastern Louisiana University. However, additional institutions are needed to solve all the engineering problems and infrastructure issues associated with ram accelerators. Therefore, the Ram Accelerator Research Program has established three areas to focus efforts to expand ram accelerator research in the United States.

Name: UConn AIAA
Description:
Founded in 2015, UConn AIAA is a student-run organization split into two teams: Design, Build, Fly (DBF) and Propulsive Landing (PL). 

Design. Build, Fly specializes in designing a functioning model aircraft for AIAA's annual competition. Each year the parameters and special requirements for the project change. This year, DBF teams are required to fit in a two foot wide parking space and carry model people and medical equipment. DBF members utilize Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) modeling, XFLR5, and Ansys to model and simulate their designs. 

On the other hand, Propulsive Landing aims to successfully land a student-built and designed model rocket using solid rocket motors. The rocket launches from a pad on the ground, and once it reaches the peak of its flight a second engine kicks in. Code written in C++ and MATLAB helps to keep the rocket stable and oriented upwards in order to safely land. Simulink is used to simulate launches and perform virtual tests. The team is currently preparing for a test launch on December 2, 2023. 

As a whole, AIAA provides students with opportunities to hone their skills, learn new ones, and connect with other students and professionals within their desired fields.

Our approach emphasizes architectures that can improve while in service, allowing capability to evolve across flights rather than being frozen at launch. Description:
Salus is developing technology to address one of the most urgent risks to the modern space economy: orbital debris. 

More than 40,000 tracked objects and over 130 million smaller fragments moving faster than a bullet, now threaten the satellites that underpin communications, navigation, Earth observation, and national security. Salus captures and contains that debris, then recovers it into reusable material rather than burning it up.

Salus is building the foundation for the first circular economy in orbit.

We are building and testing systems to capture, contain, remove and store debris and its materials to help preserve safe, sustainable access to orbit. Reliable access to space is increasingly a matter of economic and national security, and Salus is focused on the capabilities that keep critical orbits usable for the operators, agencies, and missions that depend on them.

We're currently advancing our core technology through prototype development and ground testing. If you're working on space sustainability, space domain awareness, or the future of orbital operations - whether in industry, government, or research - we'd welcome the conversation.

Governments are already funding debris-removal missions, and operators are spending billions annually on monitoring, avoidance maneuvers, and compliance. CIU fills that gap.

Our platform delivers:
AI-driven classification and clustering of orbital objects
Transparent risk scoring and prioritization
A bounty-style marketplace aligning cleanup incentives across stakeholders

Because CIU is software-first and leverages existing space situational awareness data, it scales economically as congestion grows. Its value increases with regulation, coordination complexity, and orbital density.

Turning Space Risk Into Actionable Intelligence.

We are working to mature a Hall thruster design that incorporates advanced features including magnetic shielding, and a low-cost glow discharge hollow cathode. Optimized for argon propellant, the final thruster will be integrable with CubeSat-class nanosatellites, providing a low-cost alternative to operators such as small businesses and universities who have historically had few options for on-orbit propulsion.

In pursuit of these goals, the OUROBOROS project provides students with hands-on, cutting-edge propulsion experience, contributing to the broader research community, preparing members for entry into the industry, and demonstrating the feasibility of student-developed space propulsion technologies. Name: Cosmic Tortuga
Description:
Space is humanity’s next frontier — but right now it’s a junkyard moving at 17,000 mph. One dead satellite, one lost bolt, one forgotten rocket stage can end a billion-dollar mission. We fix that. With humans in the loop and tortoises in our soul.

What we do:
1. Big Debris Relocation - Our crewed spacecraft rendezvous with large objects (dead sats, rocket bodies, mystery chunks). Pilots and robotic arms gently grab, boost to a safe graveyard orbit, and log every gram for future recycling.
2. Precision Orbit Sweeping - Swarms of orbital drones guided by human operators on-site sweep constellations clean of smaller debris. Think street-sweeper meets starfighter squadron — leaving pristine lanes for your satellites.
3. Heritage Recovery Missions - We catch historic spacecraft (think early comms sats, Apollo-era relics, even Cold-War spy birds) and bring them home intact. Delivered to museums, universities, or private collectors who want a real piece of space history on their mantle.

Every mission is human-led from a manned spacecraft. Real pilots, real engineers, real eyes on real screens — backed by autonomous drones that never sleep. Nothing is left behind. Everything we move gets cataloged, recycled, or returned.

Why humans + drones? Because space doesn’t forgive automation-only mistakes. A tortoise doesn’t rush; it verifies. We’re the same: slow enough to be safe, stubborn enough to get it perfect.

The payoff:
- Launch providers get guaranteed clean orbits
- Satellite operators get lower insurance rates
- Museums get authentic artifacts
- Collectors get bragging rights
- Humanity gets a reusable junkyard instead of a growing hazard

We’re not just cleaning space. We’re turning yesterday’s trash into tomorrow’s treasure — one careful maneuver at a time.

Name: Wavestar
Description:
Wavestar is the clearing house for space.

The orbital economy has reached the same inflection that equities reached in 1973, derivatives in 1898, and cross-border payments in 1973: bilateral settlement no longer scales. ~14,000 active spacecraft on track to 70,000+. A persistent optical mesh. In-space servicing, assembly, and refuelling that's now physical fact, not roadmap. General-purpose Linux running on satellites.

You can now buy, sell, clear, and settle five orbital asset classes the same way you'd settle equities — with one counterparty in the middle, deterministic default rules, and a public audit trail.

Wavestar runs that middle.

Four modules on one shared identity registry (did:orbit:):

→ ORCH — central counterparty for downlink minutes, ISL capacity, propellant and ISAM delivery, hosted-payload slots, and ITU-coordinated spectrum-hours
→ Terminal — Bloomberg-class system of record for satellite operators
→ Market — exchange for hosted-payload capacity
→ Attest — federated attestation network — Chainlink for orbital facts

Trust model: a permissioned Merkle transparency log (Trillian-based) plus BLS12-381 quorum signatures from a federated observer network, with hourly anchoring to Ethereum and Bitcoin for tamper-evidence. Boring crypto, vetted primitives, no novel claims.

Regulatory posture: filed to be treated as critical market infrastructure. FinCEN MSB. SEC ATS. CFTC DCO. CFTC SEF/DCM. ITU and FCC reconciliation. Four parallel tracks, no exemptions, no novel interpretations.

Founded 2026. Wyoming. Pre-launch — design-partner cohort opening Q3 2026, Series A Q4 2026.

The protocol layer will be governed by the Orbital Interchange Foundation, a 501(c)(6) non-profit, formed at month 18.

If you operate a constellation, run a ground station, hold spectrum, build hosted payloads, deliver propellant, or write rules for any of the above — we want to talk.

Malenti operates with a dual-use orientation and is registered as a U.S. government contractor (CAGE code on file). Our structure allows for integration with existing architectures while maintaining the flexibility needed for early-stage physics-driven development.

Provide operators with a deeper, more accurate understanding of the signals that shape the space environment.

TÜBİTAK ULUSAL GÖZLEMEVİ

1991 yılında yeniden belirlenen TÜBİTAK Yönetimi DPT'ye sunulmak üzere TAD Başkanlığı'ndan 5 yıllık bir Ulusal Gözlemevi kuruluş projesi istedi. Hazırlanan proje 20 Temmuz 1991'de TÜBİTAK'a sunuldu. DPT'ye iletilen proje 1992-1996 yılları arasını kapsayan yaklaşık 7 Milyar TL bütçeli bir Ulusal Gözlemevi kuruluş projesi olarak başlamış oldu.

7-11 Eylül 1992 tarihlerinde İnönü Üniversitesi'nde yapılan 8. Ulusal Astronomi Toplantısı sırasında, bu projenin yürütücülüğüne Prof. Dr. Zeki Aslan'ın önerilmesine karar verildi. Zeki Aslan'ın hazırlayıp sunduğu, 1992 yılı için 541 milyon TL bütçeli, TBAG-DPT destekli bir yıllık proje, Ulusal Gözlemevi Kurulması adı altında 1 Ekim 1992'de yürürlüğe girdi.

Gözlemevi kuruluş çalışmaları belirli bir aşamaya geldiğinde TÜBİTAK Ulusal Gözlemevi (TUG) Kuruluş ve İşletme Yönetmeliği olarak 17.07.1995 tarihli ve 22346 sayılı Resmi Gazete'de yayınlandı. Ardından 6 Ekim 1995 tarihinde de ilk müdürü olarak Prof. Dr. Zeki Aslan atandı.

2500 m yükseklikte modern bir araştırma merkezi kurmak hiç de kolay olmadı. Saklıkent'ten gözlemevine yol açılması, elektrik hattının döşenmesi, teleskop ve hizmet binalarının yapılması, gözlemevinde çalışacak teknik, idari ve araştırmacı personelinin oluşturulması gibi önemli aşamalar birer birer aşılarak 5 Eylül 1997 tarihinde dönemin Cumhurbaşkanı ve Başbakanı tarafından TUG'un resmi açılışı yapıldı.

TUG'un ilk teleskopu olan 40 cm çaplı T40 teleskopunda ilk ışık Ocak 1997'de, 150 cm çaplı RTT150 teleskopunda ise ilk ışık Eylül 2001'de alınarak gözlemevinde bilimsel gözlemler başlamış oldu.

Name: Lunar & Planetary Laboratory
Description:
Welcome to the University of Arizona’s Lunar & Planetary Laboratory (LPL).

LPL was founded in 1960 by planetary astronomer Gerard P. Kuiper, after whom the Kuiper Belt of icy objects in the outer Solar System and the Kuiper Prize (the top honor of the world’s largest organization of planetary scientists) are named. Most of the original work was based on observations using telescopes, but as the exploration of the planets expanded in scope, so did LPL. In 1973, the Department of Planetary Sciences was formed, to educate succeeding generations of planetary scientists.

Our dedicated faculty, research staff, and students come from a variety of backgrounds, including physics, astronomy, geosciences, chemistry, and engineering, but have a common interest in planets. In fact, the interdisciplinary nature of planetary science is one of its appeals for many of us, as we have to learn something of many of those other disciplines just to communicate, not to mention to succeed in understanding what is happening on, in, around, and between planets. Now, with the discovery of thousands of extrasolar planets, LPL is bringing that same interdisciplinary focus to understand whole new classes of worlds.

Name: UHU Technologies
Description:
WHAT WE DO:
We protect GPS using spatial processing techniques that can't be spoofed.

WHY WE DO IT:
We are passionate about solving emerging threats to critical infrastructure and the national defense.

ABOUT:
UHU Technologies is a privately-owned engineering research and development company that designs products to detect and mitigate GPS spoofing and jamming.

We have deep roots in signal intelligence and radio location with decades of experience producing high performance hardware. We are applying our expertise to the protection of GPS receivers for critical applications using techniques borrowed from the Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) world. Our patented techniques assure the integrity of GPS through spatial processing; for each signal we receive, we compute the angle of arrival and compare it to the known satellite location for that signal. Angle of arrival is the only signal feature that cannot be spoofed. Through additional signal processing, we spatially null (subtract) any spoofers or jammers and mitigate the threat.

Name: Western Aerospace Launch Initiative (WALI)
Description:
The Western Aerospace Launch Initiative (WALI) is a student organization at Western Michigan University (WMU).  Established in 2014 by a small group of undergraduate students interested in learning about spacecraft engineering, WALI has experienced immense growth in its lifetime.  In 2016, WALI was accepted into the University Nanosatellite Program’s (UNP) 9th iteration and participated in the program’s “Phase A” for the following two years, developing the Plasma Spectroscopy (P-Spec) mission.  This experience provided the organization with the tools necessary to establish itself at WMU and learn the fundamentals of CubeSat engineering.



In the fall of 2018, WALI was accepted into the UNP’s 10th iteration with a redefined mission named Optical Plasma Spectroscopy CubeSat (OPS-Cube).  WALI initiated a key partnership with Busek Co. and expanded its scope to explore both electric propulsion (EP) system diagnostics and CubeSat orbital maneuvers.  Through this iteration of the UNP, the organization further matured and developed into a more experienced and trailblazing team at WMU.



Again, in fall of 2021, UNP’s 11th iteration accepted WALI’s current mission called Performance of Electrospray Propulsion on Ground and in Space (PEP-GS). Electric propulsion diagnostics continue to be a main component of WALI’s mission, now with a focus on testing facility effects.



The organization is led by Principal Investigator Dr. Kristina Lemmer and assisted by Co-Principal Investigator Dr. Pablo Gomez. WALI has maintained itself on a voluntary participation basis and is currently experiencing unprecedented growth and retention rates.

Description:
Godel Space deploys autonomous AI agents to satellite payloads that orchestrate perception, triage, and communication on orbit. We turn satellites from passive sensors into intelligent, dynamically retaskable observers.

Our dual-tier architecture combines on-orbit autonomous agents with cloud-based Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) validation, producing confidence-scored intelligence that supports human decision-making.

Edge Tier: Autonomous agents running NASA/IBM Prithvi foundation models on NVIDIA Jetson platforms process multispectral imagery on-board, detecting wildfires, floods, and infrastructure changes in near-real-time without requiring full data downlink.

Cloud Tier: Google Remote Sensing Foundation Models on Vertex AI provide zero-shot detection and cross-validation, ensuring analytical depth across archival and high-resolution data.

Our orchestration layer, Trinity, coordinates between edge and cloud tiers. The edge provides real-time event triggers and prioritized downlink, while the cloud delivers analytical depth. Cross-validation between independent model families produces intelligence that defense agencies, disaster response organizations, and satellite operators can act on within minutes of acquisition.

Godel Space is a Delaware C-Corp headquartered in the Pacific Northwest. We are an EDGE AI Foundation Strategic Partner, NVIDIA Inception member, and Google for Startups Cloud Program participant selected for the Remote Sensing Foundation Model program (1 of 10 startups globally).

Name: OklahomaQuantum
Description:
Inertial sensor  provides position when GPS is unavailable. Therefore, it is used in many industries, such as autonomous vehicles, submarines, aircraft and spacecraft. However, inaccuracies or small errors of inertial sensor accumulate and increase over time, so often aircraft and submarines have to self-disclose to readjust their current position. It is often a lethal threat to missions as it reveals its location in unwanted areas.

  Quantum inertial sensors can provide near-absolute accuracy of acceleration because atoms are extremely sensitive to their environment. However, quantum technology has many shortcomings to be put into practical uses. OklahomaQauntum is developing quantum inertial sensor that is highly integrated, compact for navigation.

Name: Spargo Space
Description:
Spargo Space builds refueling infrastructure for the orbital economy.

Spacecraft today launch with a fixed propellant budget. When the tank runs dry, the mission ends — regardless of the value of the asset still on orbit. Spargo is ending the era of the single-tank spacecraft.

Our system pairs two capabilities that only work as one:
1) The depot. A 2,000 kg storable-propellant depot (hydrazine/MON-3) using industry-standard interfaces, positioned where operators need margin, not where launch schedules put it.
2) The approach. A patent-pending advisory autonomy stack for rendezvous, proximity operations, and docking. A vision-language model provides advisory perception and guidance while a deterministic safety layer retains sole control authority — intelligence in the loop, safety in command.
